Setting up the Omnisnap Action in your repository

The Action captures your pages in every engine installed on the runner, compares them and posts one comment on the pull request with the differences. It is report-only: it never fails your build, and nothing leaves the runner except the capture artifacts of that workflow run.

Two steps: the workflow on a pull request, then comments on pull requests from forks.

  • What the Action does and what it guarantees: ../specs/SPEC-ci-action.md
  • The inputs, one by one: ../action/README.md
  • The fork mechanism in depth: github-action-fork-comments.md

Before you start

  • A published release. The Action downloads its binary from the GitHub release (releases/download/<version>/…). Until the candidate v0.1.0-rc.6 is published, every job fails at the download step. There is no way around it from a consumer repository: the binary input that lets the self-test use a locally built binary only works from inside the Omnisnap repository.
  • A site that can be served on the runner. You tell the Action how to build and start it; it does not know your stack.
  • No secrets. The capture jobs need none, and no secret is exposed to the code under test.

The tables below are the starting point, not a recipe that is guaranteed to work: they are written for the versions the hosted runner images ship (Node 22, Python 3.12, Ruby 3.2, PHP 8.3), and your project may pin others.

The workflow on a pull request

Create .github/workflows/omnisnap.yml in your repository:

name: Omnisnap report          # the fork follow-up matches this string exactly

on: pull_request

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write         # to post the comment; a called workflow cannot
                                # raise the permissions its caller grants

jobs:
  omnisnap:
    uses: GerMP21/Omnisnap/.github/workflows/report.yml@v0.1.0-rc.6
    with:
      start: npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 dist
      wait-on: http://localhost:3000
      pages: |
        http://localhost:3000/
        http://localhost:3000/pricing

Two details that are easy to get wrong:

  • Do not end start with &. The Action runs it with nohup bash -c "…" in the background itself and kills it when the job ends. A trailing & leaves the server running past the job.
  • The name: matters later. The fork follow-up matches on it, character for character.

The inputs of the reusable workflow

Input Default What it does
pages (required) one URL per line, as the runner sees them
start — the shell command that builds and starts your site
wait-on — the URL the Action polls until the server answers (120 tries, one second apart)
engines every installed comma-separated engine ids (chrome, chromium, edge, firefox, webkitgtk, wpe, safari)
baseline chrome the engine every other one is compared against
runs 2 captures per engine and page
version v0.1.0-rc.6 the release tag the binary is downloaded from
macos every every runs the macOS job (and its Safari capture) on every pull request; labelled runs it only on pull requests labelled omnisnap:safari; never drops it
artifact-retention-days 7 printed in the log; the retention itself is a repository setting
setup-timeout 300 Linux: seconds the engine package downloads may take; past it the job captures without the engines it could not install

What the runner gives you

The hosted Ubuntu image (24.04) ships, among others:

Runtime Version Package manager
Node.js 22.23.4 npm 10.9.9, Yarn 1.22.22
Python 3.12.3 pip 24.0, Miniconda 26.9.4
Ruby 3.2.3 RubyGems 3.4.20
PHP 8.3.6 Composer 2.11.2

The Windows image ships Node and Python as well. Two consequences:

  • A start command that works on your machine usually works here, as long as it does not depend on a version you do not have. If your project needs Node 18 or Python 3.9, the build will fail on the runner.
  • You cannot add setup steps to the capture job. The reusable workflow owns that job, so actions/setup-node or actions/setup-python cannot run before it. Two ways out: bootstrap the version inside start (nvm and pyenv are on the image), or use the composite action in your own matrix, where the build is a step of your job and you control everything before it.

The start command, by stack

The command runs under bash on both runners (Git Bash on Windows), so keep it portable: use python rather than python3 if you need an interpreter, and avoid absolute POSIX paths.

JavaScript and TypeScript

Project start wait-on
Vite npm ci && npm run build && npx vite preview --port 3000 http://localhost:3000
Vite (static output) npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 dist http://localhost:3000
Create React App npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -s -l 3000 build http://localhost:3000
Next.js (app router) npm ci && npm run build && npx next start -p 3000 http://localhost:3000
Next.js (pages router) npm ci && npm run build && npx next start -p 3000 http://localhost:3000
Next.js static export npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 out http://localhost:3000
Remix npm ci && npm run build && npx remix-serve build/server/index.js (or npm run start) http://localhost:3000
SvelteKit npm ci && npm run build && node build/index.js http://localhost:3000
Nuxt npm ci && npm run build && node .output/server/index.mjs http://localhost:3000
Angular npm ci && npm run build && npx http-server dist -p 3000 http://localhost:3000
Astro npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 dist http://localhost:3000
Gatsby npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 public http://localhost:3000
Eleventy npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 _site http://localhost:3000
Docusaurus npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 build http://localhost:3000
VitePress npm ci && npm run build && npx vitepress preview --port 3000 http://localhost:3000
Plain static files python -m http.server 3000 --directory public http://localhost:3000

Notes:

  • npm ci needs a package-lock.json; use npm install if you do not commit one. npm ci is faster and reproducible.
  • For a single-page app with client-side routing, serve with the SPA fallback (npx serve -s) or the deep links will 404 and the capture sees an error page.
  • npx serve and npx vite preview download their package on first use; that is fine on the runner, but it costs a few seconds.
  • Check the directory your build writes to: Angular's standalone application outputs to dist/<project>/browser, Gatsby to public, Eleventy to _site, and the server frameworks to .next, .output or build.

Python static sites and docs:

Project start wait-on
Pelican pip install pelican markdown && pelican content -o output && python -m http.server 3000 --directory output http://localhost:3000
MkDocs pip install -r requirements.txt && mkdocs build && python -m http.server 3000 --directory site http://localhost:3000
Sphinx pip install -r requirements.txt && sphinx-build -b html docs build && python -m http.server 3000 --directory build http://localhost:3000

Notes:

  • Bind to 0.0.0.0. A server that listens only on 127.0.0.1 is still reachable, but a development server that picks its own host may not be.
  • Environment variables go inline: start runs through bash -c, so SECRET_KEY=dev DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=app.settings gunicorn … works. Give the app throwaway values — the capture never writes anything back.
  • A database is a problem. The reusable workflow defines no services, so there is no Postgres or Redis. Use SQLite, an in-memory database, or a migration-free code path. If the page needs a real database, use the composite action in your own matrix and add a service container there.
  • python manage.py migrate is safe to include: SQLite creates the file on the runner, and the runner is discarded afterwards.

Ruby, PHP and static generators

Project start wait-on
Rails bundle install && SECRET_KEY_BASE=dev RAILS_ENV=development bin/rails server -p 3000 -b 0.0.0.0 http://localhost:3000
Jekyll bundle install && bundle exec jekyll serve --port 3000 --host 0.0.0.0 http://localhost:3000
Hugo hugo --minify && hugo server -p 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0 http://localhost:3000
Zola zola build && zola serve --port 3000 http://localhost:3000
Laravel composer install --no-interaction && php artisan serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 3000 http://localhost:3000
Plain PHP php -S 0.0.0.0:3000 -t public http://localhost:3000

Rails and Laravel need their environment files to exist (config/database.yml with a SQLite adapter, a .env); commit a development-friendly version or create them in the start command.

Pinning a runtime version

If your project needs a version the image does not have, bootstrap it inside start:

      # Node 20 on an image that ships 22
      start: source $NVM_DIR/nvm.sh && nvm install 20 && nvm use 20 && npm ci && npm run build && npx serve -l 3000 dist

NVM_DIR is /usr/local/nvm on the Ubuntu image. For Python, pyenv or uv work the same way. Keep in mind that the same command also runs on Windows, where nvm and pyenv are not installed — so the portable answer for a project with two runtimes is your own matrix, with one job per operating system.

The two-minute budget

wait-on is polled 120 times, one second apart: the build is inside start, so it shares that budget. A Rails or Django build that takes three minutes leaves the server not yet up when the wait gives up — the Action warns, the capture runs against a dead port and every page comes back failed.

If your build is slow, use the composite action in your own matrix, where the build is its own step and the wait starts against a server that is already running:

jobs:
  omnisnap:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm ci && npm run build
      - uses: GerMP21/Omnisnap/action@v0.1.0-rc.6
        with:
          version: v0.1.0-rc.6
          start: npx serve -l 3000 dist
          wait-on: http://localhost:3000
          pages: |
            http://localhost:3000/

The pages list

  • One URL per line, absolute, as the runner sees them (http://localhost:3000/…).
  • Start with three to five pages. The wall time grows with pages × engines × runs, and the hosted runners have a 30-minute job timeout.
  • Use real content pages. A page with fewer than 50 DOM elements is treated as a bot wall and comes back unreachable; the --allow-small-pages escape hatch exists, but a page with content is the real fix.
  • The same list on every OS job: the merge step requires one job per host.
  • Pointing the list at your public URLs captures the live site instead of your branch. That is a legitimate smoke test, but it will not see your changes.
  • Paths, not just the home page: http://localhost:3000/pricing is worth more than a second copy of /.

A custom matrix instead

The composite action can be used directly, in your own matrix, and it takes the same inputs as the workflow plus out, upload, artifact-name, binary and allow-small-pages:

- uses: GerMP21/Omnisnap/action@v0.1.0-rc.6
  with:
    version: v0.1.0-rc.6
    pages: |
      http://localhost:3000/

It is referenced by path: the repository root has no action.yml, so GerMP21/Omnisnap@<tag> would not resolve.

With your own matrix you control everything before the action runs — the runtime version, the build step, a database service — and you can give each operating system its own start command.

What happens when you open a pull request

Three jobs appear in the Actions tab:

capture (ubuntu-latest)     → artifact omnisnap-Linux
capture (windows-latest)    → artifact omnisnap-Windows
merge and comment           → artifact omnisnap-merged + the comment on the PR

Every engine installed on the runner is captured on each runner — Chrome, Firefox and WebKitGTK on Linux; Chrome, Edge and Firefox on Windows — which is the point: the comment shows where your page renders differently per engine.

The comment is one markdown block, updated in place on every push. The hidden marker <!-- omnisnap-report --> is what identifies it, so a second push never adds a second comment. It carries:

  • a one-line verdict ("2 layout issues on 1 of 3 pages checked", or "No layout issues found") and a table with one row per page;
  • for each page with issues, each issue once, with the element's selector, how far down the page it is, every browser that shows it and by how much ("12 px wider" compared with Chrome), what a visitor sees, and the cause and a suggested fix when Omnisnap recognises it;
  • Not checked: browsers that were skipped and pages that failed or could not be loaded, with the reason;
  • links to the full report artifact and to the workflow run;
  • the report-only footer.

Before you open the pull request

Run the same thing locally: start your site with the same command, then point the binary at the same URLs.

omnisnap run job.json --json     # job.json lists the same pages

The local run writes the same bundle and the same report the comment will summarize, so you can see what the Action will say before spending runner minutes on it.

How to test it

  1. Put the workflow on a branch and open a pull request.
  2. Watch the three jobs. The comment lands when the merge job finishes.
  3. Push another commit to the same branch. The run repeats and the comment is updated — exactly one comment, not two.
  4. If a page shows as failed, open the omnisnap-Linux artifact: summary.json says what happened and omnisnap-progress.ndjson has the progress lines.

What usually bites

Slow Linux setup: use v0.1.0-rc.5 or later. The Ubuntu job installs WebKitGTK, Weston and the parity fonts from the Ubuntu package mirror, which can be slow depending on demand (on 2026-11-20 it served about 50 KB/s). Up to v0.1.0-rc.4 that download had no time limit of its own: it could take 15 minutes or more, or run into GitHub's 30-minute job limit and leave the report without a Linux host. From v0.1.0-rc.5 the Action caches the packages per runner image, so a later run on the same image downloads nothing, and stops downloading after setup-timeout (300 s by default): past it the job warns and captures with Chrome and Firefox. A pull request's first run still pays for the download, so on a slow day that run can lose WebKitGTK.

  • The build fails on the runner (missing environment variable, wrong version, no lockfile). The Action does not fail the job: it warns, the page is reported as failed and the comment says so. That is the report-only contract, but it means a broken build looks like a layout finding — read the job log before believing the comment.
  • Every page is unreachable. The server did not answer wait-on inside two minutes (wrong port, the build wrote elsewhere, the process exited), or the pages have too few elements.
  • Nothing is captured. Check that the download step found the release assets; the tag in version and the release tag must be the same string.
  • The site works locally and not on the runner. The usual suspects are a missing environment variable, a pinned runtime version the image does not have, and a database the runner does not have.

Comments on pull requests from forks

A pull request opened from a fork gets a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, so the job that posts the comment cannot write. The workaround is a second workflow in your repository, triggered by workflow_run after the report finishes; it runs with your token and never checks out or executes the fork's code.

1. Get the template

mkdir -p .github/workflows
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/GerMP21/Omnisnap/v0.1.0-rc.6/.github/workflow-templates/omnisnap-fork-comment.yml \
  -o .github/workflows/fork-comment.yml

2. Fix the one line it depends on

on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: ["Omnisnap report"]     # ← must equal your caller's `name:`
    types: [completed]

If your caller workflow is named something else (say Layout check), change this string to match exactly — case and spacing included.

3. Push it to your default branch

This is the hard requirement: GitHub only fires workflow_run for a workflow file that exists on the default branch. Pushing it on a branch does nothing.

The permissions it needs are already in the template:

permissions:
  actions: read
  pull-requests: write

A called reusable workflow cannot raise the permissions its caller grants, so keep that block as it is.

4. Test it

  1. Fork your repository (GitHub → Fork).
  2. In the fork, branch off the default branch and make a small, visible change — a CSS tweak is ideal, because the comment is about rendering differences.
  3. Open a pull request from the fork to the original repository.
  4. Two runs appear: Omnisnap report (the capture, with the read-only token) and then Omnisnap fork comment (the follow-up). The follow-up downloads the omnisnap-merged artifact from the first run and upserts the same marked comment.
  5. The comment appears even though the first run could not post it.

When no comment appears

Symptom Cause
The follow-up never runs fork-comment.yml is not on the default branch, or workflows: does not match the caller's name: exactly
The follow-up runs and skips The report run was not from a pull_request event, or the head repository is your repository (that path is commented by report.yml itself)
No comment, job green merged/summary.json was missing: the merge job had no bundle, or an earlier job failed — check the report run's artifacts
Resource not accessible by integration The follow-up lost pull-requests: write; check the permissions block
Comment on the wrong pull request Two open pull requests share the head branch name; the reusable workflow also accepts an explicit pr: number

The mechanism, the GitHub rules it rests on and the artifact download are explained in github-action-fork-comments.md — including why the capture job may run the fork's code with a read-only token while the comment job never does.
